title: Northstar AI x Redwood — Dedicated PoC scoping (concurrency + latency)

Northstar to share a 24h traffic/concurrency snapshot (or anonymized request logs) and the top 2–3 prompts they want to benchmark.
Redwood SE to provide a load test harness template (k6/locust) + recommended request shape (streaming on, max_tokens, typical input length).
Redwood to provision Dedicated capacity in us-east and share endpoint + auth details once the allowlist is confirmed.
Northstar to confirm whether they need VPC peering for PoC or if public endpoint is acceptable for the first week.

Stephanie Nguyen — Send PoC outline email (timeline, weekly sync invite, success metrics, pricing range/commit guardrails) — Due 2025-02-27
Maya Patel — Provide estimated peak concurrency by route (chat vs embeddings) and any existing rate-limit/429 incidents — Due 2025-02-28

transcript_text:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Northstar AI x Redwood — Dedicated PoC scoping (concurrency + latency)
Date: 2025-02-26
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Evan Brooks (Northstar AI, CTO)
- Maya Patel (Northstar AI, Platform Eng Manager)
- Jon Lee (Northstar AI, Staff ML Engineer)

---

Summary (auto-generated)
- Northstar described production spikes in concurrent requests leading to 429s and inconsistent latency on the hosted tier.
- Redwood recommended scoping a Dedicated PoC to provide predictable throughput and tighter latency SLOs.
- The group aligned on initial success criteria (p95 latency, sustained throughput, error-rate thresholds) and agreed to a weekly check-in cadence.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Current traffic + burst patterns
2) Latency targets and what “p95” means in practice
3) Dedicated PoC scope (capacity, region, isolation)
4) Load testing + benchmark methodology
5) Commercial shape after PoC (commit sizing, timeline)

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send PoC plan, sizing proposal, and schedule weekly sync.
- Northstar to send traffic snapshot + prompt set.

---

Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is Stephanie from Redwood, Markus is here as well. The goal today is to scope what a Dedicated PoC would look like given what we saw in the last call—concurrency spikes, some 429s, and then your p95 is kinda all over the place.

[00:18] Evan Brooks: Yep. Thanks Stephanie. And, yeah, that’s accurate. We’ve got… we have like normal baseline, then we have these bursts that are just, like, ridiculous.

[00:27] Maya Patel: It’s mostly top-of-hour jobs plus user traffic. The cron stuff hits at the hour and then we have customer usage that’s pretty steady.

[00:36] Markus Klein: Got it. Markus here. Before we jump into “Dedicated fixes everything,” I want to make sure we’re measuring the right things. When you say p95 latency, are we talking request to first token, or request to final token?

[00:49] Jon Lee: We look at end-to-end. Our API gateway measures from request in to full response out. But for streaming, it’s tricky because the user experience is more time-to-first-token.

[01:02] Markus Klein: Yeah, exactly. For PoC we typically track both: TTFT and total. The engine can look great on TTFT and then total depends on output length.

[01:12] Stephanie Nguyen: And just to anchor, what’s the target you’re trying to hit for your product? Like, what do you consider “good enough” for p95?

[01:21] Evan Brooks: For chat, we want first token under 400ms p95. Total… depends, but ideally under 2.5 seconds for like ~250 tokens.

[01:33] Maya Patel: Right now we sometimes see first token at 900ms to 1.2 seconds when it’s busy.

[01:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. And when it’s busy, that correlates with… is it rate limits? Is it retries? Or just queuing?

[01:47] Maya Patel: Both. We see 429s, then the client retries, then everything stacks. So it’s a little self-inflicted, but the root is the concurrency ceiling.

[01:58] Jon Lee: And we also had a couple of “model routing failed” errors. I don’t remember the exact message. It was like it fell back to another variant, but then the quality changed. That freaked out our PM.

[02:10] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s consistent with shared capacity fallback policies. Dedicated is basically: you get a reserved pool, no noisy neighbors, and we can tighten the routing and fallback behavior.

[02:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Can you give us a sense of the numbers? Like, average RPS and peak RPS, or peak concurrent requests.

[02:31] Maya Patel: Average is not bad. Like 12 to 20 RPS on chat. But peak, when the jobs hit, it can spike to 150 RPS for a couple minutes. Concurrency maybe 300-ish because responses are streaming.

[02:48] Markus Klein: 300 concurrent streams, okay. And what’s typical input/output? Like input tokens and output tokens. Rough ballpark is fine.

[02:57] Jon Lee: Input… our prompts are like 800 to 1,500 tokens. Output, most are 150 to 300 tokens, but some go to 700. There’s a long tail.

[03:09] Markus Klein: Great, that helps. And model—are you pinned to a specific one today?

[03:14] Jon Lee: We’re on… uh, Redwood’s “R-Chat” model? Sorry, I don’t remember the exact name. It’s the one you recommended in docs.

[03:22] Stephanie Nguyen: I think you’re on Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct via our catalog, right?

[03:26] Jon Lee: Yes, that. Sorry.

[03:29] Markus Klein: No worries. For that size, the burst you described, hosted multi-tenant is going to be hard to keep stable unless you accept higher queuing. Dedicated is the right lever.

[03:41] Evan Brooks: We don’t need “air gap.” We’re not like government. But we do need predictability. If we sign customers to an SLA, we can’t have random spikes.

[03:51] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. So for the PoC, here’s what I want to align on:
1) scope: which endpoints/routes, which model
2) success criteria
3) timeline
4) weekly cadence + who’s doing what

[04:05] Maya Patel: Yep.

[04:06] Markus Klein: On scope—do you want to include embeddings as well? Sometimes embeddings traffic is the silent concurrency killer.

[04:13] Jon Lee: We do embeddings but it’s separate. That’s like 80 RPS but it’s small payloads.

[04:20] Maya Patel: But it’s on the same account right now, so it competes.

[04:24] Markus Klein: That’s what I suspected. For PoC we can either isolate chat first, or we can size a pool to cover both. But mixing chat streaming and embeddings can create weird scheduling if you don’t separate queues.

[04:37] Stephanie Nguyen: What matters more for the first two weeks? Is it chat SLA, or overall throughput cost?

[04:43] Evan Brooks: Chat. If chat is stable, we can figure out embeddings later.

[04:47] Markus Klein: Great. Then I’d propose PoC is chat only, with a dedicated route, pinned model version, and no fallback except maybe within the same family if there’s an incident.

[05:00] Maya Patel: That sounds good. We had issues where it “helpfully” changed something and we didn’t want that.

[05:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. Dedicated lets us configure that more strictly.

[05:11] Markus Klein: Let’s talk success criteria. Typically we define:
- p95 TTFT under X ms at Y concurrency
- p95 total under Z seconds for a defined output length bucket
- error rate less than, say, 0.5% excluding client cancels
- no 429s from Redwood side during the test load

[05:32] Jon Lee: I’d love “no 429s.” We can tune our retries too.

[05:35] Maya Patel: We should define the test. Because in production, it’s not constant concurrency; it’s spiky.

[05:42] Markus Klein: Right. We can do two profiles:
A) steady-state: 30 minutes at 50 RPS
B) spike: ramp from 20 RPS to 150 RPS in 60 seconds, hold 3 minutes, then drop

[05:58] Evan Brooks: That second one is literally our hour mark.

[06:01] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[06:03] Markus Klein: For concurrency measurement, do you have logs you can share? Even anonymized: timestamps, tokens in/out, latency.

[06:11] Maya Patel: We can provide aggregates. We can’t send raw prompts. But we can give token counts and latency metrics.

[06:18] Markus Klein: That’s fine. For prompt content, we can use a synthetic set that matches length distribution. Or you can give us “structure” with placeholders.

[06:27] Jon Lee: Yeah we can do that. Like template prompts without customer data.

[06:32] Stephanie Nguyen: On deployment details—Dedicated for you would be in us-east, correct?

[06:38] Maya Patel: Yes. Most users are US. We’ll need multi-region later but not now.

[06:43] Evan Brooks: If it goes well, we’ll want west too, but we can start east.

[06:47] Markus Klein: Okay. For Dedicated, we can give you a single-tenant GPU pool in us-east. The PoC can run on that pool with your own endpoint. Access will still be via API key, but the backend is isolated.

[07:02] Maya Patel: Do we need VPC peering? Our security guy always asks.

[07:06] Stephanie Nguyen: You don’t need it for PoC unless it’s a hard requirement. We can do public endpoint + IP allowlist. If you want VPC later, that’s more in “Private/VPC” territory.

[07:17] Evan Brooks: For PoC, public is fine as long as it’s encrypted and we can restrict keys.

[07:23] Markus Klein: It’s TLS, and we can rotate keys. Also we can set up separate API keys for the PoC route.

[07:31] Jon Lee: On the dedicated pool, can we configure max concurrency per key? Because right now one of our internal services can stampede.

[07:40] Markus Klein: Yes, we can enforce quotas at key or project level. We can also do per-route rate limits. We’ll likely want to set something so your test harness is the only thing hammering.

[07:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Switching to commercials for a second: after PoC, if we move to Dedicated, it’s usually a monthly commit tied to reserved GPUs. But we can keep PoC usage-based with a cap.

[08:05] Evan Brooks: That’s fine. We just need a sense of the price range so we’re not wasting time.

[08:11] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. Once Markus sizes it, I’ll send a range.

[08:15] Markus Klein: Let’s talk sizing assumptions. With your numbers—150 RPS bursts, 800–1,500 input tokens, 150–300 output—my guess is you need something like 4 to 8 GPUs depending on type and batching.

[08:30] Jon Lee: Is that A100s? H100s? I don’t know what you use.

[08:34] Markus Klein: We have a few options. For PoC, we can likely use H100s in us-east depending on availability, otherwise A100. H100 gives better headroom on TTFT under concurrency.

[08:46] Maya Patel: Does batching increase latency? Because we care about TTFT.

[08:50] Markus Klein: Good question. There’s “continuous batching” under the hood. It can slightly affect TTFT if you push it too hard, but the goal is to keep TTFT low and still increase throughput. In Dedicated we can tune those knobs more aggressively without competing traffic.

[09:05] Evan Brooks: I want to be careful with “tune knobs.” We don’t want a science project.

[09:09] Markus Klein: Totally. For PoC, we’ll start with a conservative profile. If we miss throughput, we adjust. But success criteria should reflect the end result, not the initial config.

[09:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Also to reduce churn, we’ll do weekly check-ins. Same time next week? We can do 30 minutes.

[09:26] Maya Patel: Works.

[09:28] Jon Lee: I can join. I might be late sometimes.

[09:31] Evan Brooks: I’ll join at least the first two.

[09:34] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[09:36] Markus Klein: On benchmarking, do you already have a load test harness?

[09:40] Jon Lee: We have Locust scripts. It’s… not pretty.

[09:44] Markus Klein: That’s perfect actually. If you can share the shape—like concurrency model, endpoints, timeouts—we can align. We can also send a k6 starter if that’s easier.

[09:55] Maya Patel: I’d rather keep ours. But we can adapt.

[09:58] Markus Klein: Great. Key is: set client timeouts appropriately and measure TTFT. Also, streaming can cause measurement bugs if you only measure “request finished.”

[10:10] Jon Lee: Yeah, our current metric is end-to-end. We can add TTFT by capturing first chunk.

[10:17] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[10:20] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we capture what “good” looks like in writing? Like, for PoC success:
- p95 TTFT < 400ms at 300 concurrent streaming connections
- p95 end-to-end < 2.5s for 250 token responses
- 0 Redwood-side 429s during test
- error rate < 0.5%
Does that feel right?

[10:42] Evan Brooks: The TTFT number, yeah. 400ms is ideal. If it’s 450, we’re not going to walk away. But we need it under 500.

[10:51] Maya Patel: And on end-to-end, 2.5 seconds is for normal prompts. For long ones it can be higher. We can bucket.

[10:58] Markus Klein: Perfect. We’ll define buckets by output tokens: 0–300, 300–700, etc. And for input tokens as well.

[11:09] Jon Lee: Also: we have occasional tool-calling. Like function calling.

[11:13] Markus Klein: That’s okay. If it changes token counts a lot, we should include at least one tool-calling flow in the prompt set.

[11:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Another point: do you need any specific observability during PoC? Like per-request tracing or logs.

[11:28] Maya Patel: Minimal. We just need to see latency and errors. If there’s a dashboard, great.

[11:34] Markus Klein: Redwood Console can show token-level and latency breakdown per route. We can create a dedicated route tag for the PoC.

[11:44] Jon Lee: That would help. Right now we’re blind.

[11:47] Evan Brooks: Also, our finance team asked about cost predictability. That’s why Dedicated is appealing.

[11:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly. Dedicated is basically predictable cost for a known capacity. Hosted is variable and can spike.

[12:02] Maya Patel: Wait, but Dedicated still charges tokens, right?

[12:05] Stephanie Nguyen: After PoC, Dedicated is primarily capacity-based—monthly commit—though there can be overages if you burst beyond reserved. We’ll lay it out. During PoC we keep it simple.

[12:18] Markus Klein: One more technical question: are you doing any caching on your side? Like prompt prefix caching.

[12:24] Jon Lee: Not really. We considered it. But it’s complex.

[12:28] Markus Klein: Redwood has built-in prefix/KV cache depending on model and workload. In Dedicated, cache hit rates are better because the pool isn’t being flushed by other tenants. That can help TTFT for repeated system prompts.

[12:43] Maya Patel: That would be huge. Our system prompt is long and repeated.

[12:47] Markus Klein: Exactly. If your system prefix is stable, you can get meaningful wins.

[12:54] Evan Brooks: As long as it doesn’t change outputs unpredictably.

[12:57] Markus Klein: It shouldn’t. It’s a performance optimization, not a model change.

[13:01] Stephanie Nguyen: On timeline: If we start provisioning this week, we could have an endpoint early next week. Then two weeks PoC.

[13:10] Maya Patel: That works. We have bandwidth next week.

[13:13] Jon Lee: Yeah. I can run tests Monday/Tuesday.

[13:17] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll need a short list of allowed IPs and the contact who can validate connectivity.

[13:23] Maya Patel: That’s me.

[13:25] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[13:27] Evan Brooks: Can you talk about failure modes? Like if the dedicated pool goes down.

[13:32] Markus Klein: In PoC, we won’t have a formal SLA, but the infrastructure is similar. Dedicated can have HA across nodes, and we can do region failover policies. If you want a strict SLA and multi-region, that’s later. But PoC should demonstrate stability.

[13:49] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[13:51] Maya Patel: Also, what about context window? We sometimes send 8k tokens.

[13:56] Markus Klein: Llama 70B can support 8k/16k depending on variant. We should confirm which model version you’re on. For PoC, we’ll pin to the exact one you use today.

[14:08] Jon Lee: Great.

[14:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s also cover the “why not just self-host vLLM” question. I’m guessing you’ve thought about it.

[14:16] Evan Brooks: Yeah. We tried a small thing. It worked until it didn’t. We don’t want to staff SRE for GPUs.

[14:23] Maya Patel: Also capacity. We can’t get H100s easily.

[14:27] Markus Klein: Exactly. Dedicated is kind of the middle ground: you get predictable capacity but we run it.

[14:35] Jon Lee: We also looked at Together. Latency was fine but we got similar spikiness.

[14:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s consistent. Shared multi-tenant can be good until it’s not. Dedicated solves the “noisy neighbor” issue.

[14:49] Markus Klein: One thing: to hit 400ms TTFT at high concurrency, you might need to cap max_output_tokens or manage queueing. Are you okay with some guardrails?

[14:59] Maya Patel: We can set caps for the product. We already cap to 800 output tokens.

[15:04] Jon Lee: And timeouts.

[15:06] Markus Klein: Great. That will help.

[15:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Quick check: any security blockers for running PoC on public endpoint? Evan, you said it’s okay.

[15:17] Evan Brooks: For PoC it’s okay. If we go production, we’ll probably want at least SSO for the console and some audit logs.

[15:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. We can loop in our security team when you’re ready.

[15:29] Markus Klein: And we can provide SOC2 report under NDA and whatever you need, but let’s not slow the PoC.

[15:37] Maya Patel: Great.

[15:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, I’m going to recap what I heard and you tell me if I missed anything.

[15:44] Stephanie Nguyen: Northstar wants a Dedicated PoC for chat in us-east to address burst concurrency (~300 concurrent streams, spikes to ~150 RPS). Success is p95 TTFT under ~400–500ms and stable end-to-end latency with near-zero Redwood-side 429s. We’ll run two test profiles (steady-state + spike). We’ll meet weekly for check-ins. You’ll share traffic distribution and a representative prompt set (sanitized/templates). Markus will propose initial sizing and we’ll provision an isolated endpoint.

[16:18] Evan Brooks: That’s right.

[16:19] Maya Patel: Yep.

[16:20] Jon Lee: Sounds good.

[16:23] Markus Klein: One add: we should agree on what constitutes “error.” Like client cancels versus server errors. Because with streaming, cancels are common.

[16:33] Maya Patel: Yes. We cancel sometimes when the user navigates away.

[16:37] Markus Klein: Exactly. We’ll separate those.

[16:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Great point.

[16:42] Evan Brooks: Also, can you share the endpoint early even if it’s not perfect? We want to start integrating.

[16:48] Markus Klein: Yes, we can give you a dev endpoint first, then switch to final config.

[16:53] Maya Patel: As long as the model version stays consistent.

[16:56] Markus Klein: We’ll pin it.

[17:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. I’ll send an email today with next steps and propose a weekly slot. Markus will send the technical plan.

[17:08] Evan Brooks: Great.

[17:09] Jon Lee: Thanks.

[17:10] Maya Patel: Thank you.

[17:12] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

---

Notes
- Some portions of the transcript may be paraphrased due to overlapping audio and minor transcription errors.
